This study examines the production of dark matter alongside either a single top quark or a top-antiquark pair at the LHC, utilizing proton-proton collisions at $\sqrt{s} = 13$ TeV. We analyze the phenomenology of the process $pp \to t + \text{DM}$ and $pp \to t\bar{t} + \text{DM}$ within the simplified model featuring a dark matter candidate interacting with the top quark via a Higgs or gluon mediator. By employing the narrow-width approximation, we isolate the distinct kinematic signatures of single top production from top-pair production. Our findings demonstrate that the simplified model can effectively account for the dark matter component in the $t + \text{DM}$ channel, whereas the $t\bar{t} + \text{DM}$ channel remains challenging to isolate experimentally.

This work establishes the Auslander-Reiten-Serre duality within an $n$-exangulated setting. By doing so, we determine the duals of $n$-exangulated categories and the duals of $n$-exangulated quivers. Additionally, we introduce the concept of the $n$-exangulated Nakayama automorphism and demonstrate that it acts as an isomorphism between an $n$-exangulated category and its dual.

This paper establishes a theory of instrumentality for unordered treatment assignments and demonstrates its validity using historical data from the 1940s on the impact of World War II on the fields of economics and mathematics. The study analyzes the random assignment of PhD candidates to disciplines, viewing it through the lens of an instrumental variable designed to assess the effect of studying economics versus mathematics on future earnings. The analysis reveals that the apparent higher earnings potential for economists, often cited in literature, is likely an artifact of selection bias, as the war acted as a natural experiment where entry into economics was less accessible than in mathematics due to stricter requirements.

The BESIII collaboration, operating at the Beijing Spectrometer facility, has achieved energy root mean square of 4.6 GeV and an instantaneous luminosity reaching $10^{33} \text{cm}^{-2}\text{s}^{-1}$. These capabilities enable the facility to function as a $\text{J}/\psi$ factory, producing approximately $10^7$ $\text{e}^+\text{e}^-$ collision events daily. This high event rate allows for the generation of vast quantities of high-purity antiprotons and antibaryons, which can support a diverse array of innovative and high-precision scientific investigations. This document outlines the technical specifications of the BESIII apparatus, reviews current progress in $\text{J}/\psi$ region physics, and introduces several promising research avenues involving high-accuracy studies of antibaryons and exotic hadrons.

We have analyzed the evolution of hierarchical triple systems that include disks, demonstrating that angular momentum exchange between a binary disk and a single star elevates merger probabilities. This increase stems from the tendency for disks to align the binary's orbit with the disk plane, thereby reducing the inclination angle relative to a nearby third body. Such alignment fosters stronger Kozai-Lidov oscillations, which significantly boost the amplitude of these cycles and elevate the likelihood of mergers. Consequently, systems initially possessing high inclinations can experience merger rates orders of magnitude higher than those without disk-induced realignment. Furthermore, the presence of disks can amplify merger rates even in configurations lacking strong secular resonances.

We present a lattice-based framework where flatness serves as a foundational premise, leading to the derivation of the Friedmann equations alongside the cosmological constant. This constant emerges from lattice effects inherent to flat space, offering a novel perspective on its nature. Additionally, we propose an alternative lattice model based on a star graph, which yields the same space-time metric as the previously discussed lattice.

Image segmentation is a critical component of image analysis, yet traditional methods often yield unsatisfactory results when dealing with noisy images or those containing both smooth areas and distinct features. To address these challenges, this paper introduces a new variational framework for image segmentation that integrates image recovery techniques. This innovative model combines the challenges of segmentation with processes to denoise and sharpen details, thereby enhancing overall performance. The proposed approach is versatile, effectively handling general images as well as those with specific constraints, such as known boundary conditions or color data. Numerical simulations and experiments confirm the model's efficiency, demonstrating significant improvements in segmentation accuracy through the synergistic use of achievement and denoising/sharpening operations.

The angular momentum distribution of massive black holes (BHs) within the Milky Way and nearby galaxies is anticipated to be governed by the spin alignment between the parent star and the accreting material during formation, as well as subsequent gas accretion and mergers. We propose that the ultralight boson hypothesis offers an additional mechanism influencing these black hole spins through superradiant growth, which elevates the spins of BHs in the mass range of $10$ to $100\,M_{\odot}$ toward their theoretical maximum. By analyzing spin distributions across different mass bins, we can constrain the properties of such bosons. Specifically, we project that the upcoming eROSITA mission, leveraging its extensive X-ray sample of $10^6$ quasars, will achieve a $2\sigma$ sensitivity to axion-like particles with masses between $10^{-14}$ and $10^{-11}\,\mathrm{eV}$ and coupling strengths below $10^{-12}$.

The neuromorphic chip Loihi, developed by Intel, is a programmable, low-power processor capable of executing spiking neural networks (SNNs) directly on hardware. It features a detailed architecture grounded in biological neurons and synapses, supported by an extensive simulation suite. This paper introduces a software implementation of Loihi built with the Brian2 simulator, enabling the direct execution of SNNs. This implementation supports the chip's full functional scope, including detailed neuron and synaptic models, network configuration, and hardware constraints like buffer limitations. We validate this emulator through several representative examples, including a spiking version of a perceptron, a classification task, and a detailed model of a cortical microcircuit. Additionally, we compare the performance of this Brian2-based Loihi emulator against the chip's official BGL tool. Results indicate that this implementation facilitates the rapid and flexible prototyping of SNNs for deployment on hardware, while also providing a robust foundation for scientific research into neuromorphic computing architectures.

This study examines the magnetic field dynamics of a microflare occurring in the solar quiet region, utilizing high-resolution observations from the Hinode X-ray Telescope. The event, lasting approximately 100 seconds, is characterized by a noise storm source exhibiting a persistent, bright core alongside a secondary, less intense periphery. The work demonstrates that the peak X-ray luminosity correlates with specific magnetic field attributes, specifically the count of flux elements and the count of flux ropes. Furthermore, the findings indicate that the peak luminosity is governed by the magnetic field's evolution, specifically the emergence of new flux ropes and the coalescence of existing flux elements.

Atom-based sensors utilizing trapped atoms offer exceptional sensitivity for detecting electromagnetic fields, representing a significant advancement over traditional sensing methods. However, current systems rely on vacuum chambers that are bulky and difficult to integrate, restricting their application to large-scale infrastructure monitoring. This study introduces a novel compact magnetic optical trap (MOT) system, demonstrating the feasibility of a micro-scale setup with a chamber diameter of merely 3 cm. This breakthrough confirms the potential for widespread adoption of atom-based sensing technologies.

This study examines the accretion of a spherically symmetric, stationary flow of a perfect fluid with specific entropy approaching a Schwarzschild black hole. The analysis considers both cases where the flow originates from infinity and from a finite spherical boundary. It is demonstrated that, for any finite radius, the maximum possible accretion rate is finite. Furthermore, the study shows that incorporating rotational energy (vorticity) into the fluid reduces this mass accretion rate.

This study examines an atom positioned near a slender mirror, a scenario that triggers dynamic Casimir phenomena. We demonstrate that the finite inertia of an electron within this framework leads to a new form of motion-based excitation for the atom. Furthermore, we calculate the electromagnetic radiation produced by this process and show that it can be significantly amplified when the electron's inertia is taken into account.

We present the discovery of a group of giant stars with spectral types ranging from O to B in the outer regions of the nearby (5.2 kpc) and chemically young (~10 Myr) cluster Westerlund 2. Located 1.5 to 2 degrees from the cluster's center, these stars are embedded within a dense molecular cloud situated 2.5 pc away from the main group. Our findings indicate that these giants are not field stars but rather members of a secondary cluster, likely formed by the collapse of a dense molecular clump. This structure is part of a larger system that may have facilitated the formation of the primary cluster Westerlund 2.

This work examines the existence of localized solutions for a specific type of Choquard equation involving the Laplacian twice (biharmonic), set against a subcritical growth framework. The problem's novelty lies in its nonlinearity, which adheres to a exponential growth limit, alongside the absence of the standard compactness condition typically required in such analyses. To address these complexities, the authors employ a variational approach grounded in the minimax principle.

Handwritten document images, which are non-printed historical artifacts, present significant challenges for recognition systems due to noise stemming from deterioration, poor lighting, and uneven backgrounds. Although various enhancement methods exist, they often fail to address all these issues simultaneously. This study introduces a multi-scale adversarial network (MSGAN) designed to simultaneously enhance low-quality handwritten documents by restoring text, normalizing illumination, and removing backgrounds. Experiments conducted on a newly created dataset of 1,500 images demonstrate that the proposed method surpasses current state-of-the-art results in image quality metrics and achieves higher accuracy in subsequent recognition tasks.

The proliferation of digital ID documents has driven a significant increase in the demand for Optical Character Recognition (OCR) technology. While standard OCR solutions are readily available, they frequently fail to accurately extract data from Indonesian identifiers, such as National Identity Cards (KTP) and Driver Licenses (SIM), due to specific character confusion in digits '1', 'l', and 'I', as well as the nuances between the local 'o' and '0'. To overcome these limitations, this study introduces a tailored extraction system leveraging specialized preprocessing and training. We developed a dedicated dataset comprising 1,000 annotated images and trained a Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) to precisely locate and segment text regions. Subsequently, we integrated this with a trained Conditional Random Fields (CRF) model to enhance the accuracy of data field extraction. Experimental results demonstrate an overall accuracy of 94.6%, with specific precision rates of 95.1% for names, 94.6% for numbers, and 94.5% for other information.

This study introduces a novel time-averaging long short-term memory (TALSTM) technique for IEEE 802.11p physical layer channel state information (CSI) estimation. The proposed method exploits the inherent time correlations within subcarrier data across consecutive frames to enhance channel assessment. By integrating temporal dimensions into the LSTM architecture through this averaging process, the system achieves superior performance in signal reconstruction. The efficacy of the proposed scheme is validated using actual 802.11p testbed data, demonstrating significant improvements over existing LSTM models that rely solely on spatial features from the channel matrix.

Celestial image processing is vital for extracting accurate data from astronomical objects. We have implemented an advanced technique using Generative Adversarial Networks (GANs) to simultaneously improve the quality of such images and maximize the information available for analysis. We demonstrate this approach using the widely used Celestia dataset, which consists of synthetic images of the night sky.

The UAP enables a single continuous function to approximate any other continuous function within compact sets, provided sufficient data points. This principle also applies to discrete functions when enough samples are used. This paper introduces a novel, fully differentiable architecture that adheres to UAP and can approximate any continuous or discrete function given adequate training samples. This structure facilitates the creation of a feed-forward neural network that operates without calculating gradients. We present theoretical proofs demonstrating that this method achieves universal approximation and establish the convergence rate for the error as sample size increases. Furthermore, we show through experiments on synthetic data and the MNIST benchmark that this gradient-free approach attains performance comparable to standard gradient-based networks.

The ECFA Early Career Researcher's Committee (ECFA-ECYR) was established in 2021 to foster a professional community for young scholars within the field of Chinese studies. Comprising ten members, the committee is led by Chair Yaqiong Li and Vice-Chair Jiaqi Liu. This text outlines the committee's composition, its strategic framework, and a summary of its activities during the 2021 -- 2022 academic year.

Achieving precise control over light is a primary objective in the design of metamaterials and metasurfaces. This study introduces a dual metastructure capable of directing wavefronts along arbitrary trajectories, a capability that enables pivotal applications in beam steering, wavefront shaping, and optical imaging. The proposed system comprises two metasurfaces, each featuring a gradient of impedance and a gradient of capacitance, respectively. By adjusting the spatial distribution of these impedances and capacitances to counteract the accumulated phase shifts between the surfaces, the system creates a regime of phase singularity. This approach facilitates the propagation of lines of waves with confined transverse dimensions, a phenomenon termed "transverse confinement." The validity of this method is substantiated through numerical simulations of an optical setup, demonstrating the linear propagation of magnetic field energy.

The field of robotics and artificial intelligence is increasingly prioritizing "cognitive" AI systems capable of learning, reasoning, and collaborating within complex environments. A critical emerging requirement for these systems is the ability to explain their behavior to human operators, a need often referred to as providing "justification." This paper introduces a cognitive AI framework designed to facilitate extensive multi-agent learning in human-robot teams, with a specific focus on delivering both behavioral and decision-making justifications. These explanations are tailored to a human audience, employing natural language and visual representations to ensure transparency. We outline the key characteristics of these explanations and demonstrate their feasibility through a case study involving a cooperative learning scenario between a human and a robot.

This study introduces a bias-reduced estimator for the half-interquartile half-length (HIH L) of a confidence interval under a general continuous distribution. While the standard unbiased estimator for half the interquartile length relies on the second-highest order statistic, this new approach utilizes the difference between two specific order statistics. The asymptotic bias of this revised estimator is derived, and its performance is evaluated through a Monte Carlo simulation.

In recent times, connection prediction over knowledge graphs has emerged as a vital task for semantic understanding, with many contemporary methods relying on neural network embeddings to predict missing links between entities and predicates. However, these approaches often struggle to effectively capture the distributional characteristics inherent in relation structures. This study introduces a connection prediction-enhanced relation discovery framework designed to address these limitations. Specifically, we leverage the synergy between relation discovery and connection prediction to refine the latter's ability to model relation information within knowledge graphs. Our approach utilizes a neural attention mechanism to capture the associations among triples, followed by a knowledge graph completion process that refines the embedding representations of the relation data. Experiments conducted on public datasets demonstrate that our method significantly outperforms existing state-of-the-art systems in terms of F1 scores.

This study investigates quarkonium disintegration within a momentum-anisotropic, thermalized QCD medium at finite temperature and chemical potential, employing an extended quasi-debye mass framework. We analyze the in-medium properties of light, charm, and bottom quarkonia states across various angles relative to the preferred momentum direction in the N-dimensional space. Our results indicate that quarkonium dissociation is anisotropic, with the survival probability decreasing as the angle from the preferred momentum vector diminishes. Furthermore, we observe that increasing the quark mass enhances this dissociation suppression, while rising baryonic chemical potential reduces it.

We present the synthesis and structural characterization of Tb3Ru3O10, a rare terbium- and ruthenium-rich rare-earth ruthenate, which crystallizes in a monoclinic system with space group C2/m. This material exhibits a metal-insulator transition at 100 K, accompanied by magnetic ordering at 50 K. Analysis of the magnetic structure reveals that Tb ions form a 2×2×2 superstructure relative to the chemical lattice, whereas Ru moments organize into alternating-bond spin-3/2 chains. The Ru moments experience unequal internal magnetic fields, leading to a ground state defined by ferromagnetic inter-chain coupling and antiferromagnetic intra-chain interactions. Notably, the Ru moment magnitude is significantly reduced compared to the external field, and the system displays a partial disorder characterized by a 2×2×2 unit cell.

Deep neural networks are frequently employed to identify local functional representations, yet they often lack the generalizability required for practical real-world applications. This limitation arises because existing methods fail to enforce invariance to transformations such as rotation, translation, and scaling. This paper introduces a new approach to cultivate generalized local functional representations within deep architectures. We demonstrate that imposing cyclic symmetry on convolutional feature maps enables the discovery of rotation- and translation-invariant cycles within normalized convolutional features. Cycles are further refined through the application of normalized max pooling to achieve scale invariance. We validate the efficacy of these representation using two distinct applications: (1) identifying invariance to rotation and scale in conv features via the detection of cyclic structures, and (2) uncovering a cyclic pattern in the feature space of a pre-trained classifier that correlates with invariance to scaling and translation.

We introduce a semi-generative framework designed to address scenarios where the data distribution changes due to covariate shift. This approach utilizes auxiliary information about the causal structure, specifically nodes designated as causes or influences, alongside a set of high-quality training data unaffected by the shift. Our method employs a semi-generative model that integrates variational inference with conditional generative processes. It is trained on the pristine dataset to simultaneously perform covariate shift correction and density estimation. Once trained, the model can generate synthetic samples and perform likelihood evaluation on target domains affected by the shift. We validate this approach on both simulated data and real-world benchmarks, including the CelebA and YaleB datasets.

Deep learning models have achieved significant success across numerous tasks, yet their internal mechanisms remain poorly understood. This study investigates the geometric characteristics of these models to gain insight into their operational principles. We demonstrate that the feature representations generated by the network exhibit a hierarchical structure, where lower layers capture elementary patterns and higher layers encode more sophisticated combinations of these basics. Furthermore, the manifold on which data resides displays distinct properties: it possesses low intrinsic dimensionality, exhibits a clustered distribution, and shows self-similar characteristics at various scales. By leveraging these geometric properties, we can enhance the model's performance. Specifically, we apply regularization techniques grounded in the data manifold's nature to improve training, and we utilize the intrinsic hierarchical geometry of both the data structure and the network itself to develop an efficient initialization strategy.

We introduce a new class of polynomials, the Chief elements polynomials, which serve as an effective tool for analyzing the structure of finite simple groups. Using these polynomials, we further develop our earlier work on characterizing finite simple groups via their lattice of principal congruence relations. Specifically, we determine the necessary conditions for the depth of these principal congruence relations.

This study employs Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) to analyze a neural network jet classifier developed with deep learning. The investigation focuses on determining which physical characteristics most significantly influence the classifier's decision to label a jet as such. Results indicate that the classifier prioritizes jet-related properties, specifically the presence of a central quark or quantum source, high-velocity particles, and an elongated structure.

This paper introduces two new combinatorial numbers: the degenerate r-connected Stirling first kind and the degenerate r-connected Stirling second kind. We establish explicit formulas for these transformations using the degenerate binomial coefficients, alongside a formula for the inversion between these two classes of numbers. Additionally, we provide a connection to r-degenerate Bell numbers and demonstrate a relationship to the r-degenerate Stirling numbers of the first kind. The discussion further covers properties such as recurrence relations, associated generating functions, and a connection to partitions of r-degenerate subsets.

This work introduces a novel framework for characterizing the symmetry representations of space groups (SHGs) within layered materials, utilizing irreducible and local symmetries. We define two distinct approaches: (i) the "single-layer ordinary" method, which employs the conventional maximal space group symmetry for a layer, and (ii) the "double-layer exceptional" method, which utilizes maximal space group symmetry that accommodates specific irreducible symmetries for that layer. Both approaches are subsequently extended to address double layers through corresponding "double" variants. We demonstrate that irreducible-LC-based irreducible representations (IRs) of a layer can be constructed by applying the Irreducible-LCs (ILCs) of a layer's maximal space group (SHG). Furthermore, we show that the Irreducible-LCs (ILCs) of a layer's SHG can be derived from the Irreducible-LCs (ILCs) of a layer's SHG by applying the Irreducible-LCs (ILCs) of a layer's SHG to the Irreducible-LCs (ILCs) of a layer's SHG. We also provide explicit formulas for calculating the Irreducible-LCs (ILCs) of a layer's SHG from the Irreducible-LCs (ILCs) of a layer's SHG by applying the Irreducible-LCs (ILCs) of a layer's SHG to the Irreducible-LCs (ILCs) of a

We examine the relationship between a specific class of Killing vectors and the associated covariant momentum operators. This study focuses on cases where the integral curves of these vectors consist of both timelike and spacelike geodesics, analyzing the distinct properties of each. Specifically, we demonstrate that the integral paths of such vectors are real conformal Killing horizons, and we derive the corresponding covariant momentum operators for both categories. Furthermore, we establish that the operators linked to the timelike instances are Hermitian, whereas those associated with spacelike instances are non-self-adjoint.

The Hubbard sign problem, a persistent challenge in studying fermionic systems, severely restricts the applicability of Monte Carlo simulations. Although neural-network-based variational Monte Carlo has proven effective for various many-body systems, it has historically been limited by the inability of real-valued networks to represent the sign function, thus failing to fully address the Hubbard sign problem. This study introduces an innovative complex-valued neural network architecture capable of generating sign functions to mitigate such issues. We demonstrate the method's efficacy by accurately describing the sign problem in the one-dimensional Hubbard model and successfully applying it to investigate fermionization in a newly proposed three-state clock model.

We examine composite Higgs models featuring an additional scalar sector, where the vacuum expectation values of the extra Higgs bosons originate from the same symmetry-breaking scale that determines the composite Higgs vacuum alignment. This scenario offers a viable solution to the vacuum stability issues prevalent in standard composite Higgs scenarios. We analyze the phenomenology of this system within two specific realizations: an $SO(5)/Sp(4)$ model yielding a real extra Higgs, and an $SO(5)/SO(4)$ model yielding a complex one. We establish the conditions under which the tree-level potential ensures a real Higgs mass squared, and we investigate the resulting phenomenology, including constraints from LHC searches for extra Higgs bosons and deviations in electroweak precision observables.

Virtual reality (VR) has become a pivotal tool for investigating how perception changes, particularly due to its ability to deliver immersive, multisensory experiences. This paper introduces a novel theoretical framework suggesting that perception shifts within VR stem from the brain's attempt to reconcile conflicting sensory data with established prior knowledge. We propose that the "shadow aspect" of these alterations lies in their capacity to reveal the specific prior expectations held by users.

The BigScience Multilingual Framework introduced a collection of multilingual models trained on 13 languages, covering 95% of global speakers. This study explores extending the framework to include additional languages by adjusting it for two specific cases: Zulu and Vietnamese. We present the development of new resources, including monolingual corpora, translation pairs, and multilingual datasets, for these linguistic contexts. Our analysis examines how incorporating Zulu and Vietnamese impacts performance on the existing languages and introduces the capabilities within the new linguistic domains.

Fragmentation events involving massive, spinning cores can yield binary systems, a process examined here through the lens of a simplified two-body model. In this framework, the parent core's rising total mass drives the expansion of its surface, while the dual system forms when two fragments detach. Conservation of angular momentum dictates that the resulting masses and separation distance are determined by the core's initial spin. We analyze how the mass of the new two-body system evolves as a function of the parent core's mass and rotation rate. Our findings indicate that the resulting mass is always lower than that of the progenitor, with the deficit growing as the core spins faster. Furthermore, we observe that the mass contained within the smaller fragment increases with the parent core's mass and reaches a maximum when the core is critically spinning; beyond this threshold, the fragment becomes the entire core itself. Additionally, we explore the implications of these mass distribution characteristics on the formation of black hole-neutron star binaries.

We introduce a new method termed "Autonomous Component Analysis" (A.K.A. m-ar-K-Fast), designed to extract multiple non-orthogonal features from data. This approach builds upon the Non-Linear Kernel Feature Mapping (A.K.A. N-K-F) technique introduced in 2018, which was originally intended for single-feature extraction. Our extension allows the user to specify the number of desired independent components, denoted as m. The resulting features are both self-explanatory and statistically independent, making them highly effective for downstream machine learning applications. Our analysis demonstrates that this technique serves as a universal approximator capable of representing any continuous function within the space defined by m independent components. Furthermore, we provide theoretical convergence guarantees for the algorithm and establish its robustness against outliers.

This paper addresses a fundamental question in finite model theory: determining the relative expressive power of two specific logics, Choiceless Polynomial Time (CPT) and Choiceless Polynomial Time with Durations (CPTD), on ordered graphs. We demonstrate that the two differ in a specific scenario: there exists a pair of $K$-diagrams (where $K$ is a fixed constant) that CPTD can distinguish, whereas CPT cannot. Our proof relies on a reduction to known results concerning the complexity of distinguishing these diagrams under bounded degree constraints. Additionally, we examine the connection between these logical distinctions and demonstration complexity within the extended polynomial calculus, specifically regarding the refutation of unsatisfiable $\{0,1\}$-formulas.

This paper presents a new infinite family of rings that are $\sigma$-elementary for every integer $\sigma \ge 1$. These rings are constructed as subrings of the field of $p$-adic numbers, $\mathbb{Z}_p$, where $p$ is a prime number.

Assertion generation serves as a critical component of automated testing. While assertion messages that fail indicate discrepancies between actual outcomes and expected results, the precision of these failures hinges on the correctness of the assertions themselves. The verification process for assertions typically involves a human tester who confirms that an expected value aligns with prior knowledge or system specifications upon failure. However, this manual approach becomes unfeasible for assertions that cannot be checked by humans due to their complexity or volume. This study introduces a method for automatically detecting issues in assertions that lack human verifiability. The proposed approach initially converts the assertion into Natural Language Processing (NPL) representations, subsequently employs semantic analysis to pinpoint potential problems, and finally utilizes a classification model to determine the specific type of assertion error. Experiments conducted on the Assertion Corpus demonstrate that this methodology achieves an F1 score of 0.82.

Identifying real-time events using geo-tagged social media data is a critical task for monitoring public occurrences like natural disasters and traffic congestion. This study introduces a new methodology for detecting and forecasting events by employing a spatial-temporal convolutional network to analyze the sequential flow of check-ins. The system was evaluated against two datasets: one capturing real-time information from a major global social network and another comprising historical records of major incidents in New York City. The findings demonstrate that the proposed system achieves superior performance in both event identification and temporal prediction compared to existing methods.

This work introduces a swift methodology for analyzing the CMB-induced distortion of galaxy luminosity distributions, specifically targeting the bispectrum. The approach involves applying the galaxy bispectrum filter to simulated sky maps that incorporate both the Cosmic Microwave Background and Large Scale Structure (LSS) data. We evaluate the efficacy of this technique by examining the signal arising from the CMB–LSS cross-correlation within a $\Lambda$CDM framework, alongside noise contributions from the CMB itself and the LSS. The study further investigates how various tracers of Large Scale Structure are impacted by the anisotropies of the CMB.

This paper presents a Bayesian estimation framework designed to deliver posterior distributions with certifiable accuracy when dealing with potentially corrupted data. By utilizing a rigorous lower bound on the standard deviation of data-dependent noise, we establish bounds for the squared Bayes risk under the $L_2$ loss function. These findings are applicable to scenarios involving arbitrary outliers and also extend to scenarios involving Gaussian noise with a known lower bound on the variance. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by implementing it in two practical domains: 1) robust clustering through a novel method called the robust expectation-maximization (EM) algorithm, and 2) robust principal component analysis (PCA), where we provide an efficient algorithm capable of handling outliers and out-of-distribution samples.

Digital rumors have severely disrupted China's efforts to combat the COVID-19 pandemic. This study examines the dissemination dynamics and influence of such rumors on digital social platforms within China. By analyzing Weibo data from the early stages of the outbreak, we identified the temporal patterns of rumor spread and evaluated their impact on users' emotional states. The findings reveal that rumor activity peaks approximately 10 days after initiation before declining, and that exposure to these narratives significantly intensifies anxiety among individuals.

This study examines the effects of spectral dimensionality reduction on the categorization of hyperspectral imagery. We employed various unsupervised and supervised techniques for spectral feature extraction, utilizing them as inputs for a subspace learning algorithm. Results indicate that spectral dimensionality reduction can enhance classification performance, with the optimal outcomes achieved through supervised methods. Furthermore, we assessed the efficacy of these reductions on real-world data by comparing them against standard benchmarks using the Indian Pines and Indian Meadows datasets.

This paper introduces a general methodology for deriving weaker logical frameworks from existing ones, with the specific aim of creating more efficient implementations. We demonstrate the utility of this approach by applying it to the OLogon framework, resulting in a reduced version that retains full compatibility with original code while yielding significant gains in both execution speed and memory usage.

In this study, we validate and improve protein framework models by comparing them with experimental NMR proton chemical displacement data. The proton chemical displacement values for the protein backbone were simulated using quantum mechanical calculations, while those for a protein-water complex were simulated using molecular dynamics combined with quantum mechanical calculations on proton positions. These simulations were performed on proteins of varying sizes, specifically ubiquitin, the T4 lysozyme C-terminal domain, and MS2 capsid protein. The results indicate that experimental NMR data for amide protons aligns most closely with models where the protein backbone amide protons are positioned 2.9 ± 0.5 Å from the protein surface. Furthermore, the calculated proton chemical displacement distributions for both protein sizes and protein-water complexes were compared against experimental distributions. The analysis demonstrates that the protein-water complex model provides a superior representation of experimental data compared to the protein framework alone.

Deep learning has become a standard in the classification of high-dimensional data, such as images and audio, largely due to its ability to automatically extract features from raw inputs. This process typically involves training a model to map raw data to a specific class by minimizing a loss function that quantifies the discrepancy between actual and predicted labels. While the selection of an appropriate loss function is critical for optimal performance, deep learning frameworks offer numerous alternatives, making this choice complex. This study investigates how different loss functions impact the accuracy of deep neural networks across various datasets, specifically focusing on the CIFAR-10 image classification task. Results indicate that modifying the standard cross-entropy approach with a weighted variant can enhance accuracy, particularly in scenarios involving class imbalance.

We establish a connection between parquet theory and many-body perturbation theory within an expansion of the S-matrix, governed by a specific Hamiltonian that incorporates both parquet and counterterm operators as its components. This Hamiltonian yields a systematic series of S-matrix coefficients, which can be rigorously demonstrated to align exactly with those obtained through traditional parquet theory.

The study introduces a novel approach utilizing time-dependent density functional theory (TD-DFT) and time-dependent many-body perturbation theory (MBPT) to investigate the mechanism of excitonic condensation in TiSe$_2$. This method enables the calculation of the exciton dispersion and the determination of the critical temperature ($T_c$) for condensation. Furthermore, the research examines the impact of the excitonic gap on the material's optical properties.

Urbanization has intensified the need for effective public safety measures, prompting the deployment of various tools to bolster community security. Among these, text-based reporting systems (TTS) have gained prominence, enabling citizens to submit incident details directly to authorities via mobile devices. Although TTS offers the immediate advantage of real-time data transmission, the vast volume of unstructured entries often hinders the extraction of actionable intelligence. Consequently, this study introduces a novel framework designed to analyze the interactions between TTS participants and the system's automated dispatchers. By leveraging Natural Language Processing (NLP) and Machine Learning (ML), the proposed approach uncovers concealed patterns within dispatcher communications, specifically targeting the identification of emerging threats and evolving behavioral trends among users. Furthermore, the research evaluates the impact of these interactions on overall system engagement and proposes targeted interventions to optimize participant experience. Ultimately, this work seeks to deepen the comprehension of TTS operational dynamics, thereby facilitating enhanced security outcomes and heightened community protection.

We examine a two-dimensional nematic superconductor, a state defined by gapless nodal quasiparticles and spontaneous time-reversal symmetry breaking. Our analysis reveals that, despite the presence of these nodes, the linear-temperature dependence of spin susceptibility arises from Cooper pair effects rather than individual quasiparticles. We derive an expression for the spin susceptibility in terms of the nematic order parameter, which allows for its calculation via angle-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (ARPES) data.

Engaged education represents a dynamic pedagogical approach where educators and learners collaboratively establish the educational environment, its objectives, and the methods to achieve them. This paper introduces a novel framework called Minimax Engaged Education, designed to resolve conflicts arising from the divergent preferences of these two parties. The proposed model is formulated as a specific variant of the Minimax Correlated Equilibrium problem, for which we have developed an efficient algorithm capable of identifying a solution in polynomial time.

This study examines the evolution of musical complexity in Western art music and pop songs spanning the last 200 years. By analyzing audio recordings, we measure complexity using the spectral entropy of the short-time Fourier transform (STFT) magnitude. We observe that the average complexity of pop music has risen significantly from 1960 to 2010, a trend not seen in art music over the same period. Furthermore, the distribution of complexity values for both genres has become increasingly skewed toward lower levels throughout history.

This paper examines a general class of reinforcement schemes that encompasses both the multi-arm bandit problem and models involving independent or coupled random walks on graphs. We establish a broadened version of the "one-armed bandit" theorem, demonstrating that under specific conditions, the system's allocation of trials to various options asymptotically mirrors the behavior of a standard single-option bandit. Applying this extended result, we derive the conditions necessary for asymptotic optimality within the multiple-entry framework.

This study investigates how to create light and shadow within a room through a team of robots, where each robot functions as an individual agent equipped with a computational model of a playful environment. The research examines a multi-agent scenario where a computational model of harmony guides the agents' actions, directing them to move strategically to generate delightful patterns of illumination. The paper outlines a methodology for achieving agent coordination through harmony, presents a specific harmony function tailored to this lighting context, and evaluates the resulting robotic behaviors using an experimental harmony metric.

Current reinforcement learning (RL) approaches for robotic manipulation often depend on human demonstrations to define reward functions. However, creating these rewards is frequently constrained by a lack of time and patience. To address this, we introduce a novel method that enables engineers to define rewards by ranking pre-generated RL policy clusters, supported by an interactive visual interface. This system allows users to provide global feedback on policy performance without needing to observe specific actions, thereby facilitating the fine-tuning of policy behaviors. We validate this approach on the task of bimanual drawer opening, showing that it effectively converges to a high-performing policy with significantly fewer interactions compared to existing techniques.

This paper presents a characterization of conciseness within the Smyth domain order specifically for core-compact spaces, alongside the introduction of the conciseness property within ordered structures.

This study introduces a novel class of vortex loops in two-dimensional liquids, where loops move with a constant average velocity. Unlike previously observed dissipative loops in viscous fluids or accelerating loops in ideal vorticity-conserving models, these loops maintain steady motion because their propagation aligns with a specific aim direction defined by the system's initial conditions. This phenomenon arises in systems possessing strong repulsive interactions, which support a perfect 2D liquid state characterized by long-lived quasiparticles and negligible vorticity diffusion. Consequently, the loops' velocity remains stable over extended durations, a durability that increases as the loop size grows.

This study introduces a novel hybrid approach for generating multivariate forecasts by merging the advantages of deep learning and traditional econometric models. We adapt the enhanced inverse likelihood weighting (ELILW) technique, a method originally developed for nowcasting, to forecast over longer horizons. In this framework, multivariate predictions are constructed by merging forecasts from various models, with weights dynamically adjusted based on each model's forecast errors relative to historical data. We employ a feedforward neural network to generate forecasts for the remaining variables whenever data for any single observation is missing at a specific point in time. This proposed method, designated as NN-ELILW, is evaluated using both simulated datasets and real-world applications involving US stock market and macroeconomic time series.

The article examines the theoretical and experimental status of $\tau$-lepton physics, a field that has become a focal point for the LHCb and Belle II experiments. It is argued that theoretical predictions for $B$-meson decays into $\tau$ leptons are essential for interpreting LHCb's results, yet current models exhibit significant discrepancies with these observations. The text outlines the theoretical efforts aimed at resolving this puzzle, while also addressing the prospects for reducing experimental uncertainties through the analysis of $B$-meson decays into $\tau$ leptons and pions by LHCb. Furthermore, the study explores the potential of measuring the anomalous magnetic moment, $a_\tau$, and the electroweak parameters $\sin^2\theta_W$ and $\alpha_{EM}$ using $\tau$-lepton decays. These investigations, conducted using $e^+e^-$ colliders like SuperKEKB, are expected to achieve sensitivities comparable to those achieved by the historic MARK-II detector at PEP in the 1990s.

This study presents a computational and experimental investigation of wave generation in a rotating annulus driven by horizontal temperature differences, with the primary goal of benchmarking the large-eddy simulation (LES) code RotFlow against established experimental data. The study examines two specific aspect ratios, $\alpha = 0.5$ and $\alpha = 0.25$, utilizing temperature contrasts of $\Delta T = 2.5$ K and $5.0$ K. The experimental results are compared with numerical simulations, which utilize the Raible and Rotunno (2004) boundary conditions and are benchmarked using the same temperature contrast values ($\Delta T = 2.5$ K and $5.0$ K) and aspect ratios. The study finds that the wave dynamics observed in the simulations align closely with experimental observations, particularly in the $\alpha = 0.5$ case where the flow is characterized by a wave number of $n=2$. However, in the $\alpha = 0.25$ case, the flow exhibits a transition to a higher wave number ($n=3$) at a critical Ekman number of $E_c = 1.2 \times 10^{-4}$. The study concludes that the wave dynamics observed in the simulations are consistent with experimental observations, particularly in the $\alpha = 0.5$ case where the flow is characterized by a wave number of $n=2$. We introduce a parametrization of the Poisson process that enables straightforward computation of the tail index and the measure of intensity beyond a high threshold within heavy-tailed scenarios. Utilizing this framework within a Bayesian estimation context, we derive posterior distributions for the Poisson process intensity and the tail index by conditioning on the transformed data. The Poisson process is reparametrized such that the resulting transformed data are independent, with each component following a marginal distribution that can be predetermined. The effectiveness of this approach is demonstrated through numerical simulations and a practical analysis of the S\&P 500 index.

In the domain of Reinforcement Learning (RL), corruption refers to the deliberate manipulation of training data by adversaries with the intent of degrading the performance of learned policies. While the potential risks of such attacks are well-understood, existing literature has largely concentrated on online RL frameworks, leaving offline RL—where training occurs using static historical datasets—vulnerable and under-explored in this context. This paper introduces a novel, model-free, sample-efficient, and offline approach designed to build robust agents capable of withstanding data tampering. The proposed framework integrates two primary components: an outlier detection module that identifies and removes anomalous, potentially compromised data samples, followed by a policy optimization strategy that incorporates uncertainty estimates to ensure robust decision-making. Empirical evaluations across various environments demonstrate that this method consistently outperforms current baselines, exhibiting superior resilience against both subtle and overt forms of corruption.

This work examines the controllability of the one-dimensional heat equation with time-varying boundary controls. It is demonstrated that a sufficient criterion for achieving a uniform temperature distribution (zero state) at a terminal time $T$ involves the sign consistency of the logarithmic derivative of the spatial weight function. Additionally, for instances where this logarithmic derivative exhibits a finite number of singularities, it is established that reaching the target state remains feasible provided the control time $T$ is sufficiently large.

Detecting and identifying categories of out-of-distribution (OOD) texts is essential for numerous natural language processing (NLP) applications. This work introduces a unified framework that simultaneously addresses OOD detection and the classification of unseen text categories. We define a new task called "classification of in-domain text categories" (CDO) to guide the identification of specific OUD categories. The proposed approach employs a generative framework that models both the target CDO categories and the OOD categories. By leveraging this generation process, the framework can identify OOD inputs and, upon detection, predict their specific category. We evaluate this method on the newly established CDO task and the newly released OOD detection benchmark, MedOUD. Results demonstrate that this approach outperforms existing baselines in both OOD detection and CDD performance.

Brownian molecular engines, which operate by converting inelastic electron tunneling into mechanical work, have recently attracted significant attention. This study establishes a statistical mechanics framework for these systems, utilizing a dynamical model for a single molecular ratchet connected to a quantum dot. We demonstrate that the system's internal energy increases as a function of the quantum dot's chemical potential. Furthermore, we show that the system functions as a heat engine, transforming thermal fluctuations into coherent motion and performing work on its surroundings.

Term transducers serve as a generalization of both resynchronization and display machines, functioning as a mechanism to synchronously resynchronize pairs of terms within a specific synchronizable display language. This work examines the resynchronization capabilities of these devices when restricted to one direction. We establish that the resynchronization of a term transducer in the unidirectional (one-way) sense is equivalent to the existence of a display machine that can resynchronize terms in a one-way direction. Additionally, we demonstrate that the resynchronization of a term transducer can be achieved in a one-way direction if and only if it is display machine-free.

This study examines the efficiency of computing generalized convolutions defined as $C = A \circ B$, where the entry $C_{i,j}$ equals the dot product of the $i$-th row of matrix $A$ and the $j$-th column of matrix $B$. While this operation is a broad framework encompassing standard matrix multiplication, element-wise (Hadamard) product, and even set-bitwise operations, it has long been recognized that these generalized forms do not necessarily adhere to the same computational lower bounds as the classical version. This paper introduces an algorithm capable of performing generalized convolution with a time complexity of $O(n^{\omega-1}n \log^2 n)$, where $\omega$ represents the exponent for standard matrix multiplication. This represents a significant acceleration compared to the brute force approach, which requires $O(n^3)$ time.

The initial discovery of a T-dwarf in 1995 marked a pivotal moment in the field of brown dwarf research. Since that era, a wealth of observational data has been gathered, revealing that the object, designated GJ 229B, possesses the most extensive dataset among all T-dwarfs. This study employs the APOLLO retrieval code to analyze the spectral characteristics of GJ 229B, utilizing the most comprehensive collection of observations available to date. Our findings indicate that the atmosphere of GJ 229B is characterized by a high metallicity and a super-solar carbon-to-oxygen ratio, with a temperature of 770 K and a pressure of 1.0 bar. Furthermore, the atmospheric composition is rich in methane, ammonia, and water vapor, while carbon monoxide exists only in trace amounts. The analysis also reveals a significant presence of clouds, with the cloud base situated between 0.1 and 1.0 bar. These results are consistent with previous studies, which employed diverse modeling techniques to interpret the spectra of this historic brown dwarf.

This study investigates the existence of an $0^{-+-}$ state by analyzing the decays $J/\psi \to \gamma \eta'$ and $J/\psi \to \gamma \eta'$, a process that is forbidden by charge conjugation in the Standard Model. We evaluate the relevant amplitudes using both the hadronic loop model and the gluonic hybrid model. Our calculations demonstrate that the branching ratio for the $J/\psi \to \gamma \eta'$ decay lies within the $10^{-4}$ range, a magnitude sufficient to be observable. These findings suggest that experimental observation of this decay channel could provide compelling evidence for an $0^{-+-}$ state, thereby supporting the presence of an exotic vector meson.

This study examines the parameters $\phi_s$ and $\Delta\Gamma_s$ within the $b\bar{b}$ system using data from 3 fb$^{-1}$ collected by the LHCb experiment at a center-of-mass energy of 7 TeV. The analysis leverages time projections of decays into $f_0(1500)\pi^+\pi^-$ and $f_0(1500)\pi^-\pi^-$. By employing a fit that isolates the time-dependent contribution of $\phi_s$, the result $\phi_s = -0.20^{+0.23}_{-0.21} \pm 0.06$ rad is determined. The sensitivity to $\Delta\Gamma_s$ is evaluated through the same decay channels, yielding a sensitivity of $0.045$ fs$^{-1}$.

This study introduces a well-mixed framework for forecasting infectious disease transmission within an urban bus environment. We demonstrate that this approach offers superior performance compared to a network model that accounts for direct person-to-person contact, which is typically used to model infection risk on buses. Additionally, we evaluate the effectiveness of a well-mixed framework in supporting the evaluation of mitigation strategies. Our results indicate that this framework provides a valuable tool for assessing potential measures, such as enhanced ventilation and the use of face masks, to reduce the probability of disease spread within public transit buses.

This study utilizes the shell-model to investigate the forbidden $\beta$-decay properties of $^{135,137}$Te, specifically calculating $\beta$-decay half-lives, $ft$ values, and log $ft$ values. These calculations rely on the widely adopted universal shell-model interaction, $V_{UCR}$, and wave functions derived from experimental energy levels. The computed theoretical $ft$ values align well with experimental measurements, demonstrating that $V_{UCR}$ is highly effective for describing $\beta$-decay properties in the $^{124}$Sn to $^{144}$Sn isotope chain. Furthermore, the $\beta$-decay matrix elements for $^{135,137}$Te are analyzed, and the corresponding nuclear wave functions are examined.

The double-faced auction operates as a mechanism to transform goods into information, enabling the exchange of that data for other goods; however, it suffers from authentication issues because participants can submit fabricated bids. This paper introduces an authentication solution utilizing blockchain technology, specifically enhancing the double auction model to create what is termed an authenticated variant. The study evaluates this new model by comparing its outcomes with the traditional version under conditions of both honest and strategic participant behavior.

This work investigates the bottomless semileptonic decay of $B_s \to D_s \ell \nu_\ell$ within the framework of Heavy Quark Effective Theory (HQET). We determine the meson form factors by employing light-cone sum rules (LCSR) and analyze the resulting $B_s \to D_s$ transition form factors. Our findings are contrasted with previous theoretical estimates and experimental measurements.

This study introduces a fresh perspective on the combinatorics of compositions by linking composition numbers to the topological degree of a specific mapping. The authors establish a bridge between compositions and the degree of degree-one maps, focusing on a periodic nonexpansive curve within the context of the degree. They derive a formula for calculating the degree based on the parity of the sum of the parts and the specific values of those parts. Furthermore, the work extends this approach to handle compositions involving repeated parts, yielding a summation formula that utilizes binomial coefficients.

This paper introduces a novel variant of dynamic mode decomposition (DMD), termed kernel DMD (kernel DMD), which enables the extraction of time-scale-specific coherent structures from data. This approach is particularly advantageous for analyzing complex systems characterized by nonlinearities and noise. The proposed framework enhances the robustness of spectral estimation by employing a nonlinear mapping to a higher-dimensional feature space, thereby facilitating the identification of dominant patterns. The method's efficacy is demonstrated through applications to both linear and nonlinear systems, with specific examples including a linear time-invariant system and the Lorenz attractor.

This paper introduces a novel framework for analyzing chess openings, leveraging data from online platforms to assess both their complexity and similarity. To analyze structural similarity, we employ graph theory, representing each opening line as a graph where nodes correspond to board positions and edges represent legal moves. We then apply an approximation algorithm for the graph edit distance problem to compute distances between these opening graphs. For measuring intricacy, we utilize the concept of logical depth, defined as the computational effort required by a universal Turing machine to regenerate the depth-specific information contained within a state. Finally, we validate our findings by comparing these metrics against Grandmaster tournament statistics.

Pale dwarfs, which are dense clusters of millisecond pulsars (MSPs), offer an ideal setting for discovering these objects. This study introduces a novel method to derive the mass and distance of an MSP system by analyzing the autocorrelation of pale dwarf light curves. By applying information criteria, we can determine the optimal autocorrelation lag, which corresponds to the system's light-travel time. Furthermore, by incorporating the amplitude of this autocorrelation, we can calculate the binary separation, effectively yielding the product of the system's mass and distance. Although individual values for mass and distance cannot be isolated through this technique alone, the approach successfully provides these parameters for MSPs within pale dwarfs that were previously unmeasured.

This work examines the motion of mechanical systems described by a generalized Lagrangian framework, which incorporates both local and specified nonlocal temporal dependencies. We derive the corresponding Euler-Lagrange equations, derive the associated conservation laws for quantities that are inherently nonlocal, and analyze the stability of equilibrium points within this context.

This study introduces a method for generating and acquiring 3D forms, utilizing a VR environment equipped with a haptic device. The system allows users to create shapes through direct manipulation in 3D VR space, employing a "point-by-point" drawing strategy where points are defined by their coordinates. These points are then transformed into surface representations, such as meshes or parametric models, by matching them against a database of pre-existing forms. To support this, the research also presents an algorithm for retrieving 3D form data based on point-cloud input. The effectiveness of the proposed approach was verified through experiments, and the study concludes with suggestions for future developments.

The James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) is designed to detect the minute changes in position of exoplanets caused by gravitational interactions with other planets within their systems. To achieve this, the mission requires highly precise ephemerides, which depend on accurately measuring the transit times of planets using a global network of ground-based observatories. This study utilizes transit observations of HD 80606 b, a highly eccentric planet, collected by 11 telescopes across 14 sites over a span of 10 years. The resulting data allow for a significant refinement of the planet's orbital parameters, reducing uncertainties in the semi-amplitude of the eccentricity ($K_e$) and mean anomaly ($M_0$) by factors of 10 and 30, respectively. These enhanced ephemerides are expected to substantially boost JWST's ability to identify and characterize future signals from exoplanet systems.

This study examines the stability of a spherically symmetric, static, self-gravitating ideal fluid governed by a linear equation of state, $P = (\gamma - 1)\rho c^2$, where $\gamma$ is an adiabatic index. The analysis demonstrates that while the fluid remains stable against both entropy and vorticity disturbances when $1 < \gamma \leq 5/3$, it becomes unstable if $\gamma > 5/3$. This critical threshold aligns with the condition for the Chandrasekhar limit, indicating that the fluid undergoes gravitational collapse beyond this point. The findings are consistent with Chandrasekhar's earlier conclusion that white dwarf stars collapse once their mass surpasses a specific critical value.

We revisit the extremal black hole problem within Iyer-Wald's framework, deriving various upper limits on mass for both electrically charged and gravmagnetically charged configurations. Our analysis reveals that, in the presence of an external electromagnetic field, mass constraints differ between gauge-dipole aligned and anti-aligned scenarios. Furthermore, we examine how misaligned angular momentum vectors influence these bounds.

Although deep neural networks (DNNs) have proven effective in addressing numerous machine learning challenges, they often demand extensive training data and computational resources. Consequently, investigating sample efficiency is critical for DNNs to unlock their full potential. This study introduces the End-Influence Investigation Push (EIIP), a novel framework designed to enhance training sample efficiency. EIIP operates by identifying and prioritizing the most informative training samples for the DNN, thereby accelerating learning from fewer data instances. This approach involves two key components: the End-Influence Metric (EIM) and the EIM-based Reservoir Sampling (EIRS). The EIM assesses a sample's potential impact on final model performance, while EIRS ensures a diverse selection of high-impact samples during the training process. Empirical results across three computer vision and one audio recognition task demonstrate that EIIP significantly boosts training sample efficiency. Specifically, the method achieves a 2.3-fold reduction in data requirements for image classification and a 2.5-fold reduction for speech recognition, with comparable performance levels.

We introduce a novel framework for particle physics and cosmology, termed Vibrant Mechanics, which derives particle properties from the vibrational modes of a 12-dimensional internal space. This space is characterized by its signature of (10,2) Poincaré symmetry, allowing the use of null vectors to define null geodesics that support particle vibrations. The model accounts for the hierarchical structure of the universe, including the cosmological constant, and outlines a vibrational origin for dark matter and dark energy.

We introduce new parameterized algorithms addressing both single and bipartite upward planarity testing. For a directed graph $G=(V,E)$ rooted at $r \in V$, a drawing is considered upward planar if it is planar and every edge edge travels upward; additionally, if every edge from any vertex is upward, the drawing is termed upward planarity. We present an algorithm that decides upward planarity for a graph with $n$ vertices in $O(2^k n)$ time, where $k$ represents the maximum in-degree. This study introduces a new task called episodic memory-guided navigation, which involves leveraging guided recollections to explore an environment and locate a goal. We propose MemoNav, an agent designed to achieve this by selectively retrieving salient past experiences from a memory bank, a process we term "remembrance." We evaluate several remembrance strategies, including those based on saliency, confidence, and counterfactual reasoning, and compare them against both baseline methods and human performance. Our findings reveal that our approach surpasses existing algorithms and achieves results comparable to humans. Additionally, we release MemoNav as an open-source project, complete with extensive analyses of its decision-making processes and memory usage.

This paper examines the evolution of compact base stations (BSs) from the 4G era through projected 6G networks, with a specific focus on small cells. It outlines the historical background, current status, and future trajectory of small cells, analyzing their critical role in enabling 6G. The study details the anticipated evolution of the Radio Access Network (RAN) and the overall cellular architecture, highlighting the integration of large-scale MIMO and millimeter-wave (mmWave) communications. Furthermore, the authors explore the concept of the "Green Cell," emphasizing energy efficiency as a primary objective for 6G. The work concludes by addressing future research directions and potential challenges associated with small cell deployment in next-generation mobile networks.

This paper introduces a new concept, the "framework," which serves as a hypergraph analogue to both graph and simplicial complexes. We establish the existence of a specific category of frameworks and demonstrate that it is equivalent to a previously defined category of simplicial complexes. Additionally, we prove the closure of frameworks under the operations of subhypergraphs, joins, and complete complements. The study further defines the concept of minimal frameworks and proves that every framework can be constructed through a linear ordering of its simplicies, combined using the operation of set-theoretic joins. Finally, we examine the concept of the "complete" framework and establish an important result: the complete frameworks within this new structure correspond exactly to simplicial complexes defined on hypergraphs.

We investigate the connection between the operator product expansion (OPE) and the light-cone cone expansion within the framework of four-dimensional quantum field theory. By examining the behavior of the OPE in four dimensions, we demonstrate that it inherently incorporates light-like separations, thereby establishing an intrinsic relationship with cone expansions. This connection, however, is complicated by infrared divergences, which obscure a direct mapping between the two expansion methods. To address this issue, we employ the subtracted OPE, enabling a more precise analysis of how the subtracted form relates to light-like correlations and the cone expansion. We further explore the correspondence in the context of quantum mechanics through a simplified model, where we show that the operator structure of the cone expansion can be explicitly derived from that of the OPE.

Direct decay from the Hoyle state ($^ {12}$C*$_{0^{++}}$) to the ground state offers a means to test models of nuclear structure. This study reports the initial observation of such events using the experimental setup at the ISOLDE facility at CERN. The data, collected via a Time Projection Chamber (TPC), reveals the complete decay trajectory of individual alpha particles, enabling the determination of their kinetic energies with high precision. The study's primary outcome is a nearly background-free measurement of the direct-decay width ($\Gamma_{\rm dd}$) of the Hoyle state, yielding a value of $0.92^{+0.24}_{-0.21}$ eV. This result aligns closely with theoretical predictions and provides a robust determination of the total Hoyle-state width ($\Gamma_{\rm tot}$) as $0.92^{+0.24}_{-0.21}$ eV.

This study investigates oscillatory and tip-splitting instabilities in quasi-brittle materials using a cohesive zone model. By examining the dependence of oscillation amplitude and wavelength on loading levels and rate, we analyze how these factors influence the system. The findings indicate that elevated loading rates enhance both the amplitude and wavelength of generated oscillations. Furthermore, a material length scale is identified that dictates the critical loading rate required to trigger oscillatory failure. Additionally, the research explores the transition from oscillatory patterns to tip-dividing (branching) instability as the loading rate increases.

This study examines communication across a finite-state environment subject to noise at both encoder and decoder, where feedback is permitted. The system operates under a constraint that encoders must remain within specific energy limits relative to the channel state, defining an allowable set of states. Decoding is assumed to be state-aware, meaning it incorporates current channel state information. The primary objective is to determine the optimal feedback capacity, which represents the maximum reliable data rate. The analysis derives both lower and upper bounds for this capacity, which converge to exact values in the absence of channel states or when such states follow a uniform distribution. The findings are applicable to practical scenarios such as wireless transmission, where channel conditions fluctuate and feedback mechanisms are present.

This study examines spin-singlet topological superfluidity within the attractive Rashba Hubbard model, employing both mean-field theory and dynamical mean-field theory (DMFT). We demonstrate that, unlike in weak-coupling regimes where DMFT results align with mean-field predictions, the inclusion of strong local correlations within the DMBA approach uncovers a novel topological superfluid ground state characterized by $d$-wave symmetry.

This paper outlines the submissions made by the UvA-NLPC team for SemEval-2021 Task 9 (SEM-TAB-FACTS). Our approach focuses on two sub-tasks: verifying the accuracy of individual cells within tables and assessing the overall correctness of table summaries. To achieve this, we utilized a graph-based table cell value extraction framework alongside two distinct large language models. The system achieved the highest performance on the summary verification component, finishing in the top two positions overall.

We introduce a new class of irrational numbers termed "intricate," defined by the property that their simple continued-fraction coefficients grow exponentially. The set is sufficiently rich to express any other intricate number using only $\pi$, $e$, and potentially other standard mathematical constants. For example, $\sqrt{2}$ can be represented as $e^{\pi} + \pi e + \pi$, and $\sqrt{3}$ as $e^{\pi} + e + \pi$. The name "intricate" was selected to evoke both complexity and an element of mystery.
